pr_title: don't do cgroupvs2 if any controller is already in use for cgroupsv1
pr_body: when running in a container on a host that is using cgroup1, we can't use only unified cgroup, since it won't contain any of the cgroup controllers, as they're all in use by cgroup1, so we must use cgroup1/hybrid in the container as well.
pr_comments:
> superseded by #20705 I think?

well, no; I do agree with @yuwata change to prevent starting oomd if the memory cgroup isn't available (and skip the test) but that doesn't fix the core problem, which is that systemd is mounting /sys/fs/cgroup as a unified cgroup inside a container where none of the cgroup controllers are available to cgroup2.

I do need to rework the patches on top of main though, I'll push a new patchset today or tomorrow.

Not sure I follow? the container manager should really pre-mount `/sys/fs/cgroup` for us, depending what type of hierarchy they picked? We can't possibly guess what the chosen way to set things up is, we need some form of communication there, either by mounting things, or by telling us via kernel cmdline or so, or by using our built-in.

Which container manager is this?

> Not sure I follow? the container manager should really pre-mount `/sys/fs/cgroup` for us, depending what type of hierarchy they picked? We can't possibly guess what the chosen way to set things up is, we need some form of communication there, either by mounting things, or by telling us via kernel cmdline or so, or by using our built-in.

well i don't think it's unreasonable for the container manager to pre-mount /sys/fs/cgroup as appropriate, but as you know the [container interface spec](https://systemd.io/CONTAINER_INTERFACE/) says 

> Either pre-mount all cgroup hierarchies in full into the container, or leave that to systemd which will do so if they are missing.

So...I think systemd should try to get it right.

> 
> Which container manager is this?

It's lxd, and yes nspawn does get things right, but obviously nspawn is part of systemd so of course it does what systemd expects :)

I think that lxd only mounts /sys/fs/cgroup when the host kernel doesn't include cgroupns support, though @stgraber can correct me on that.

However, my understanding is that kernel cgroupns support provides isolation for cgroups inside the namespace, meaing in the container /proc/*/cgroup will correctly refer to cgroups inside the namespace, not the host cgroups; but I believe that the kernel still has the hard limitation of any cgroup controller that has been 'dedicated' to cgroup1 being unavailable in a unified cgroup2 mount, even inside a cgroupns. I might be wrong about that, but a quick review of the kernel code did seem to indicate that (and quick tests seem to confirm it).

> that's a bit too magic for case. what happens if you run a cgroup 1 host with all controllers disabled?

i'm rebasing/reworking the patch, but having all controllers disabled is a fairly simple case; systemd should just mount a unified cgroup, since neither cgroup1 nor hybrid or unified will have any controllers at all in that situation.

Unless you are set against this, I was going to open a issue to track it, instead of reusing the already-closed issues, or just keeping this PR without a bug.

Note that we document the model of delegation explicitly, and say what should be provided to container payloads depending on the cgroup mode the container manager picks. See:

https://systemd.io/CGROUP_DELEGATION

The section about "systemd as Container Payload". 

If you don't prepare a cgroup setup for systemd, then it will pick whatever it was told to do during compile time. That logic matters, since that's what we need to do when booting up on a bare kernel. I am not convinced we should add black magic that tries to unreliably detect what it shall setup.

We documented this since a long time, so that container managers can implement this and things *just* work. It's a pity that your container manager makes this hard, but I am not convinced it would help to work around that now. The thing is: this is mostly a problem that is self-made by lxd, is a problem that will fix itself sooner or later anyway as cgroupsv1 gets phased out more and more, and fixing this in systemd is not going to fix old payloads anyway. The latter is important: what's the benefit of adjusting systemd to match lxd's behaviour if this means you ave to then fix 1 million payloads to upgrade to that systemd version — if instead you could just fix lxd once and make things just work — with all payloads from the last years just magically working, in a clean and well-defined way.

So I am still very much against adding something like this, as this is mostly a heuristic, not more.

> but I believe that the kernel still has the hard limitation of any cgroup controller that has been 'dedicated' to cgroup1 being unavailable in a unified cgroup2 mount, even inside a cgroupns. I might be wrong about that, but a quick review of the kernel code did seem to indicate that (and quick tests seem to confirm it).

Note that on cgrouspv1 controller delegation is not safe and not supported by systemd nor the kernel (you can in fact define configs that way that will confuse the kernel very much, if you ignore this). If you want controller delegation use cgroupsv2.

>  It's a pity that your container manager makes this hard,

well...just to be clear, it's not "my" container manager, I don't work on it at all... ;-)

>  what's the benefit of adjusting systemd to match lxd's behaviour if this means you ave to then fix 1 million payloads to upgrade to that systemd version

I think it's relevant because the specific problem here is *new* systemd running in a container on *old* host system. While Debian switched to default to unified back in 2020, Ubuntu is just now changing the default over to unified in the upcoming release.

This means all old host systems have hybrid (or plain cgroup1) cgroups, which will cause problems when running containers with newer Ubuntu releases.

Since most environments, especially enterprise environments, run older code on their bare metal hosts, with newer code in VMs and containers, this PR should address the most likely short-term situation. In fact, many very large enterprise environments are extremely hesitant to upgrade *anything* on hosts, so updating lxd (and/or maybe other container managers - I don't know how others behave) might take longer to roll out for many existing users, instead of updating systemd in new container instances.

In any case, I'll rebase/rework this and push it again, and you can take another look, just in case. And I'll hold off on opening a bug for this, unless you'd like me to.
test failure looks unrelated, TEST-24-CRYPTSETUP appears to have failed when waiting for its device to appear.

I just noticed the loop in `cg_any_controller_used_for_v1` should perhaps skip controllers that are generally ignored by systemd, i.e. check only controllers from `enum CGroupController`. Not a big deal, it can be fixed later or worked around by explicitly passing `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1`.

> I just noticed the loop in `cg_any_controller_used_for_v1` should perhaps skip controllers that are generally ignored by systemd, i.e. check only controllers from `enum CGroupController`. Not a big deal, it can be fixed later or worked around by explicitly passing `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1`.

comments: I think the core problem is any container running on a host where cgroup1 is in use (either cgroup1 only, or hybrid) can't use cgroup2, since all the cgroup controllers will be in use by the host cgroup1, and the container's cgroup2 mount will lack any cgroup controllers.
